column3: Mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips with hamartomatous GI polyps is Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, which is not listed; polyps cause bleeding and intussusception.
The small bowel digests and absorbs, the colon mainly absorbs water and ~1 L of ileal content enters the colon daily. B12 and bile salts are absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Thrombosis occurs at the SMA origin; pain out of proportion to signs is the hallmark. Ischaemic colitis favours the splenic flexure and may stricture; angiodysplasia is right-sided.
D
Ileocolonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsy confirms Crohn disease histologically; MR enterography (or small-bowel contrast studies) then defines extent and strictures.
After IV rehydration, intussusception is reduced by an image-guided enema (air/pneumatic now preferred to barium); surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.
Admit, rehydrate and stop the causative antibiotic; oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is now first-line for C. difficile, metronidazole only where these are unavailable.
C
In Africa, Asia and South America sigmoid volvulus is the commonest cause of large-bowel obstruction; in the West it is colorectal cancer. Hernias mainly obstruct the small bowel.

Management of left iliac fossa pain: you are asked by your senior colleague to devise the treatment plan for the elderly man with acute diverticulitis described above. What is the most appropriate treatment plan?
Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy (± appendicectomy)
Fever with marked RIF tenderness and rebound means peritonitis; with inconclusive ultrasound, diagnostic laparoscopy is safer than waiting or a CT in a child.
Radiological (air or contrast) enema reduction after an abdominal film
First-line treatment of uncomplicated intussusception is image-guided air (pneumatic) or contrast enema reduction; surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.
CT with contrast is the investigation of choice for a suspected diverticular abscess and guides percutaneous drainage.
Diarrhoea with fever after a recent admission and antibiotics suggests C. difficile colitis; of these options, oral metronidazole (oral vancomycin is now first-line).
Air or contrast enema reduction
A stable infant with intussusception (colic, ‘red-currant jelly’ stool) is treated first by image-guided air/contrast enema reduction.
Six weeks of bloody mucoid diarrhoea with urgency in a young man is ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise: stool cultures, then colonoscopy with biopsies.
Acute LIF pain, fever and raised WCC/CRP in a 65-year-old is acute sigmoid diverticulitis; confirm with CT if severe or uncertain.
Swinging fever with a pericolic abscess on CT in a stable patient without peritonitis: CT-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics.
Abdominal pain, fever and tachycardia on day 5 after colectomy is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise: start IV antibiotics with resuscitation, then CT or re-laparotomy.
The jejunum is thicker walled, redder, with prominent plicae and less lymphoid tissue, and secretes most digestive fluid; the ileum is thinner, paler, with Peyer patches.
Before appendicectomy in a girl of reproductive age, a pregnancy test is mandatory; other imaging rarely changes a clear clinical decision.
Intermittent inconsolable distress, vomiting and ‘red-currant jelly’ stools in an infant is ileocolic intussusception; ultrasound shows a target sign.
E
Appendiceal adenocarcinoma with lymphatic invasion needs a right hemicolectomy for nodal clearance; appendicectomy alone suffices only for low-grade mucinous neoplasms (LAMN).

A 37-year-old man with a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis has a sessile polyp with high-grade dysplasia 10 cm from the anal verge. Which operation is most appropriate?
High-grade dysplasia in UC marks a field change: total proctocolectomy, with an ileoanal J-pouch to preserve continence.

A 33-year-old man with Crohn disease has severe abdominal pain and fever: HR 130/min, BP 105/62 mmHg, temperature 38.9 °C, WCC 32 000/mm³; plain films show a markedly dilated colon. Which operation is most appropriate?
Toxic megacolon failing medical therapy is treated by subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy, leaving the rectum for later reconstruction.
Adhesions are the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction in the West, followed by hernias and malignancy.
Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum (bleeding, obstruction from intussusception or volvulus, diverticulitis or perforation) needs resection.
B
Severe unilateral lower abdominal pain in a young woman with normal inflammatory markers and negative β-hCG suggests an ovarian cyst (rupture or torsion); pelvic ultrasound.
